### Lindsay Edmonson

Your exploratory data analysis of the team datasets go here.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

glaciers <- read.csv("../data/processed/glaciers.csv")
```

```{r}
ggplot(glaciers, aes(x = aspect_sec)) +
  geom_bar()
```

> This charts the frequency of each direction that the glacier surface faces with 1 being due north.
> Most of the glacier surfaces face north but several also face north east and northwest.
> The fewest amount of glaciers face south.

```{r}
ggplot(glaciers, aes(x = slope_deg, y = maximum_elevation)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")
```

> This plot shows the relationship between the slope of a glacier and its maximum elevation.
> It is a positive but moderate relationship and mostly linear.
> Most slopes are between 0 and 40^o^ and most max elevations are between 500 and 3000 m.

```{r}
glaciers |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = area_km2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100)

glaciers |> 
  filter(area_km2 < 1) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = area_km2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100)

glaciers |> 
  summarize(median_area = median(area_km2),
            mean_area = mean(area_km2))

glaciers |> 
  arrange(desc(area_km2)) |> 
  head(10)
```

> This plot shows the area of all of the glaciers in the data set.
> Upon closer inspection, most of the data points fall below 0.5 with a median of 0.296.
> The data is very skewed to the right because the mean area is 4.09.
> So, most of the glaciers are less than half a km^2^ in area with a few data points that are very high with the biggest glacier being 3362.6 km^2^.
